I’ve been working these 12 mu in Quzhou for 45 years, and at 62 I know every corner of the land. With just my wife and me in the household, labor is the bottleneck, so I split the farm between the reliable wheat-maize double crop and the cash-earning cotton. This year I’m keeping 7 mu in wheat-maize and 5 mu in cotton. The wheat is already in the ground from last autumn; I rotary-tilled and planted an improved variety, and now I’m managing it through to June. I’m targeting about 500 kg/mu, so I’ll topdress to bring the total nitrogen to about 20 kg/mu, with 8 kg phosphorus and 5 kg potassium. I have the well, so I’ll irrigate four times—winter water, jointing, heading, and grain fill. I’d rather pay the pumping cost than risk a drought. Two pesticide sprays will cover weeds and any fungus.

For the summer maize, there is no time to till after wheat harvest in early June; I always use no-tillage direct seeding with a hybrid variety. I expect 550 kg/mu, applying about 18 kg N, 5 kg P, and 5 kg K per mu, and irrigating twice at the critical silking stage. Two pesticide applications handle the weeds and armyworm.

The 5 mu of cotton is my main cash crop, but it is back-breaking work—topping, pruning, and hand-picking. I’ll rotary-till in April and plant a hybrid variety. I expect around 270 kg/mu of seed cotton if I stay on top of the bollworms. That means about 13 pesticide sprays through the season. I’ll irrigate three times—at planting, flowering, and boll set—and apply roughly 16 kg N, 6 kg P, and 7 kg K per mu. My education helps me keep the rates straight, but I’m still a smallholder: I stick to what works, adjust a little from last year, and never overextend on labor or cash.
